questions.question: What is @WebMvcTest and what does it load?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest Purpose
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot test slice that loads only the web layer — controllers, filters, and MockMvc — without starting services, repositories, or the full application context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to test controllers without loading the full application
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for controller tests, loading too much context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @WebMvcTest requires @MockBean for the service layer because services are not loaded

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot test slice annotation designed specifically for testing your controller layer. When you put it on a test class, Spring Boot loads only the web-related beans: your @Controller and @RestController classes, @ControllerAdvice for exception handling, @JsonComponent, WebMvcConfigurer, filters, and the MockMvc infrastructure. It does NOT load your @Service, @Repository, or any other non-web beans.

You can target a specific controller by passing it as a parameter: @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class). This is a good practice because it makes it explicit which controller you're testing and avoids loading controllers you don't need.

Because services are not loaded, you must mock them with @MockBean. If your OrderController depends on OrderService, you declare @MockBean private OrderService orderService in your test, configure its behavior with Mockito's when().thenReturn(), and then use MockMvc to send HTTP requests to the controller and assert on the HTTP response.

Compared to @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest is significantly faster because it doesn't load the full context. It's the right choice whenever you want to test request mapping, request validation, response formatting, HTTP status codes, or error handling at the controller level without involving real business logic.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Loads only web layer: controllers, filters, MockMvc — no services or repositories
Use @WebMvcTest(YourController.class) to target a specific controller
Service dependencies must be mocked with @MockBean
Much faster than @SpringBootTest for controller-focused tests

questions.question: How do you write a basic @WebMvcTest to verify a GET endpoint returns 200 OK?
questions.title: Basic @WebMvcTest GET Request
questions.direct_answer: Inject MockMvc with @Autowired, stub the service with @MockBean, then call mockMvc.perform(get("/path")).andExpect(status().isOk()).

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on ability to write a controller test — this is the most commonly asked coding question in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the MockMvc fluent API or forgetting to stub the @MockBean service
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the test structure methodically: setup (MockBean stub), perform, andExpect

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A basic @WebMvcTest for a GET endpoint has three parts: setup, perform, and assert. Let me walk through each.

First, the class setup: annotate with @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class), inject MockMvc with @Autowired private MockMvc mockMvc, and mock the service with @MockBean private OrderService orderService.

Then in the test method, you stub the service: when(orderService.getOrder(1L)).thenReturn(new Order(1L, 'Coffee')). This ensures your controller gets a real object back even though the service is a mock.

Finally, perform the request and assert: mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Coffee")). The perform() method sends a mock HTTP request. andExpect() chains assertions on the response.

Important imports: MockMvcRequestBuilders.get() and MockMvcResultMatchers.status() and jsonPath(). Spring Boot's test starter includes all of these in the org.springframework.test.web.servlet package.

For a POST request, you'd use post("/orders").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(objectMapper.writeValueAsString(dto)), and then assert status().isCreated() for a 201 response.

This is a very commonly tested pattern in fresher interviews — interviewers often ask you to write this from memory or recognize what a given test is doing.

sections.title: Key Points
content: mockMvc.perform(get("/path")) — sends mock HTTP GET request
.andExpect(status().isOk()) — asserts HTTP 200
.andExpect(jsonPath("$.field").value("expected")) — asserts JSON response body
Stub the @MockBean service before calling perform() so the controller has data to return

questions.question: What does @WebMvcTest NOT load and what do you have to provide yourself?
questions.title: What @WebMvcTest Excludes
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest does not load @Service, @Repository, @Component, or any non-web beans — you must provide these as @MockBean in the test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what the slice actually isolates, and what to do about missing beans
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting NoSuchBeanDefinitionException and not knowing to add @MockBean
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that even security configuration may need to be addressed — security beans are loaded by default in @WebMvcTest

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest is deliberately narrow — it only loads web-layer beans. The following are NOT loaded: any @Service annotated class, any @Repository, any general @Component, JPA/Hibernate configuration, database connection pools, and any other infrastructure beans.

If your controller depends on a service, and you forget to provide that service as a @MockBean, Spring will fail to create the controller bean because its constructor argument (the service) is missing. You'll get a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException or an UnsatisfiedDependencyException at test startup.

The solution is always @MockBean: add @MockBean private YourService yourService to the test class. Spring Boot creates a Mockito mock and registers it as a bean in the test context, satisfying the controller's dependency.

One thing to be aware of is Spring Security. By default, @WebMvcTest does load your security configuration if you have @EnableWebSecurity in your project. This means your tests might get 401 or 403 responses unless you handle authentication in the test. You can either use @WithMockUser from the spring-security-test library to simulate a logged-in user, or use @WebMvcTest with security disabled by excluding the security auto-configuration.

This is a common gotcha for freshers — tests suddenly fail with 401 and they don't understand why.

sections.title: Key Points
content: @Service, @Repository, @Component are NOT loaded — mock them with @MockBean
Missing a @MockBean causes UnsatisfiedDependencyException at test startup
Spring Security IS loaded by default — tests may get 401 without @WithMockUser
Use @WithMockUser from spring-security-test to simulate authenticated requests

questions.question: How do you test a POST endpoint with a request body using @WebMvcTest and MockMvc?
questions.title: Testing POST Endpoint with MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: Use mockMvc.perform(post("/path").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content(json)).andExpect(status().isCreated()) to test a POST endpoint with a JSON body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical MockMvc knowledge — POST testing is slightly harder than GET and commonly asked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to set contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), which causes a 415 Unsupported Media Type
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the request construction and the response assertion, and mention using ObjectMapper to serialize the request body

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Testing a POST endpoint with MockMvc requires a few more steps than a GET, mainly because you need to provide a request body and set the content type header.

First, in your test class, inject the ObjectMapper: @Autowired private ObjectMapper objectMapper. Spring Boot auto-configures ObjectMapper, and @WebMvcTest loads it for you.

In the test method, create your request DTO object, then serialize it to JSON: String json = objectMapper.writeValueAsString(createOrderRequest). Then perform the request: mockMvc.perform(post("/orders").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).content(json)).andExpect(status().isCreated()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").exists()).

The critical things to get right: contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) sets the Content-Type header. Without this, Spring can't deserialize the request body and will return 415 Unsupported Media Type. The content() method takes the JSON string as the request body.

For the assertion, isCreated() checks for HTTP 201. If your endpoint returns the created resource in the response body, you can chain jsonPath assertions to verify specific fields.

You should also stub your @MockBean service: when(orderService.createOrder(any())).thenReturn(new Order(1L, 'Coffee')). Without the stub, Mockito returns null by default, which may cause a NullPointerException in your controller.

content: post("/path").contentType(APPLICATION_JSON).content(jsonString) — builds POST request
Use @Autowired ObjectMapper to serialize DTOs to JSON strings
Missing contentType() causes 415 Unsupported Media Type
Stub the @MockBean service with when().thenReturn() to avoid NullPointerException

questions.question: How do you test that a controller returns a 404 when a resource is not found?
questions.title: Testing 404 in @WebMvcTest
questions.direct_answer: Stub the @MockBean service to throw a ResourceNotFoundException, and assert .andExpect(status().isNotFound()) in the MockMvc call.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to test error/exception paths — not just the happy path
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only testing happy path success cases, ignoring error scenarios
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @ControllerAdvice/GlobalExceptionHandler and how it ties into the test

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Testing error scenarios like 404 is just as important as testing the happy path, and it's a common interview question because it shows you think about failure cases.

The approach depends on how your application handles the exception. If you have a @ControllerAdvice that catches a specific exception — say ResourceNotFoundException — and returns a 404 response, then you test it by making the @MockBean service throw that exception.

Here's how: stub the service with when(orderService.getOrder(99L)).thenThrow(new ResourceNotFoundException("Order not found")). Then perform the request: mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/99")).andExpect(status().isNotFound()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.message").value("Order not found")).

The key is that @WebMvcTest loads @ControllerAdvice beans, so your exception handler is active in the test. The mock service throws the exception, the controller propagates it, the @ControllerAdvice catches it and maps it to a 404 response, and MockMvc asserts on that response. The full exception handling chain is tested.

If your controller handles the exception inline — for example, catching it and calling return ResponseEntity.notFound().build() — then you'd do the same stub but the @ControllerAdvice isn't involved.

Always test your error paths in controller tests. Interviewers notice when candidates only write happy path tests.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Stub the @MockBean service to thenThrow() the exception that triggers the error response
@WebMvcTest loads @ControllerAdvice — exception handlers are active in the test
.andExpect(status().isNotFound()) asserts HTTP 404
Test error paths as well as success paths — shows thorough thinking

questions.question: How do you use jsonPath() in MockMvc to assert on the response body?
questions.title: Using jsonPath() in MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: jsonPath("$.fieldName").value("expected") asserts that the JSON response body's field equals the expected value — it uses JsonPath expressions to navigate the JSON structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical MockMvc assertion knowledge — jsonPath is the most common way to check response bodies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing jsonPath syntax or only asserting the status code without checking the body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both simple field assertions and nested/array assertions

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
jsonPath() is a MockMvc result matcher that lets you navigate and assert on JSON response bodies using JsonPath expressions, which are similar to XPath but for JSON.

The most basic usage is: .andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1)) — the dollar sign represents the root of the JSON object, then dot notation navigates to the field. For a response like {"id": 1, "name": "Coffee"}, you'd assert jsonPath("$.name").value("Coffee").

For nested objects — say the response is {"order": {"id": 1}} — you'd use jsonPath("$.order.id").value(1).

For arrays — say {"items": ["a", "b"]} — you'd use jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("a") to check the first element, or jsonPath("$.items").isArray() to check that the field is an array, or jsonPath("$.items", hasSize(2)) to check the array length (this requires Hamcrest).

You can also use .exists() to check that a field is present, and .doesNotExist() to verify a field is absent from the response. This is useful for verifying that sensitive fields like passwords are not exposed in API responses.

The imports you need are import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.jsonPath and the Hamcrest matchers from import static org.hamcrest.Matchers.*.

sections.title: Key Points
content: jsonPath("$.field").value("expected") — asserts a field equals a value
jsonPath("$.nested.field") — navigate nested objects with dot notation
jsonPath("$.array[0]") — index into arrays
jsonPath("$.field").exists() and .doesNotExist() — assert field presence/absence

questions.question: Can you use @WebMvcTest without specifying a controller class?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest Without Specifying a Controller
questions.direct_answer: Yes — @WebMvcTest without a parameter loads all controllers in the application, but it's better practice to specify the controller to keep tests focused.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the annotation's default behavior and best practices
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not specifying the controller and then wondering why @MockBean is needed for an unrelated controller's dependencies
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the practical reason for specifying the controller: reduces test setup and makes intent clear

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Yes, you can use @WebMvcTest without specifying a controller class. When you do that, Spring Boot loads all the controllers it finds in your application. This is technically valid but generally not recommended.

The problem is that when all controllers are loaded, you need @MockBean for every service that any controller in the project depends on. If you have 10 controllers each with 2-3 service dependencies, your test class ends up needing 20-30 @MockBean declarations even though you're only testing one endpoint. The test becomes cluttered with mocks that aren't relevant to what you're verifying.

When you specify the controller — @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) — Spring only loads that controller. You only need @MockBean for the services that OrderController specifically depends on. The test is minimal, focused, and easier to understand and maintain.

This follows the single-responsibility principle for tests: each test class tests one controller. If you have OrderController and UserController, you'd have OrderControllerTest with @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) and UserControllerTest with @WebMvcTest(UserController.class).

Always specify the controller. It's a small thing, but it signals to interviewers that you write tests intentionally and understand what you're loading.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Without a class parameter, @WebMvcTest loads all controllers — valid but not recommended
Always specify the controller: @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
Specifying reduces the @MockBean requirements to only that controller's dependencies
One test class per controller keeps tests focused and maintainable
